title_original: The Anatomy of Remembrance: María Magdalena Campos-Pons and Kamaal Malak in Koyo Kouoh’s In Minor Keys
excerpt_original: Through their collaboration, KaMag, María Magdalena Campos-Pons and her husband, musician and sound artist Kamaal Malak, transform painting, monumental sculpture, sound and scent into a multisensory tribute to Koyo Kouoh and Toni Morrison in Anatomy […]

blocks.text: Through their collaboration, KaMag, María Magdalena Campos-Pons and her husband, musician and sound artist Kamaal Malak, transform painting, monumental sculpture, sound and scent into a multisensory tribute to Koyo Kouoh and Toni Morrison in ‘Anatomy of the Magnolia Tree for Koyo Kouoh and Toni Morrison’ (2026). Presented within In Minor Keys , their work explores the spiritual dimensions of remembrance, the enduring influence of Black women and art’s capacity to offer solace in an unsettled world.
Brendon Bell-Roberts

In Anatomy of the Magnolia Tree for Koyo Kouoh and Toni Morrison (2026), monumental magnolia blossoms command the exhibition space, their oversized petals unfolding into sculptural forms that seem to hover between botanical reality and the imagined. Behind them, a large-scale diptych reveals a richly layered world of human figures, flowers and foliage, where the faces of Koyo Kouoh and Toni Morrison emerge from an intricate landscape of memory and transformation. Low musical frequencies resonate through the room, while the fragrances of guava, sugarcane, citrus and herbs permeate the air. The installation is at once exuberant and contemplative, enveloping visitors in an environment where painting, sculpture, sound and scent converge. Created by Cuban-born artist María Magdalena Campos-Pons and her husband, musician and sound artist Kamaal Malak, working together as KaMag, Anatomy of the Magnolia Tree for Koyo Kouoh and Toni Morrison transforms remembrance into an immersive sensory encounter. Maria Magdalena Campos-Pons, installation view in Anatomy of the Magnolia Tree for Koyo Kouoh and Toni Morrison (2026), Giardini main pavilion. Photo courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts.

blocks.caption: Maria Magdalena Campos-Pons, installation view in Anatomy of the Magnolia Tree for Koyo Kouoh and Toni Morrison (2026), Giardini main pavilion. Photo courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts.

blocks.text: Presented in the Giardini’s Central Pavilion as part of In Minor Keys , the Venice Biennale exhibition conceived by the late Koyo Kouoh, the installation occupies a particularly poignant position. Kouoh died in May 2025, leaving her curatorial team to realise the exhibition she had envisioned. Rather than functioning as a conventional memorial, Campos-Pons and Malak’s work gives physical and sensory expression to the values that animated Kouoh’s thinking: generosity, attentiveness, collective care, and the possibility of finding beauty amid profound uncertainty.

The magnolia provides the central visual and conceptual language. Associated with the American South, its beauty is inseparable from a landscape shaped by histories of enslavement, racial violence and the resilience of Black communities. Its flowering also suggests regeneration, an insistence on life that connects the installation to Kouoh’s vision of an exhibition attentive to quieter forms of resistance, contemplation and renewal.

The relationship between Kouoh and Morrison is central to this conception. Morrison transformed the possibilities of literature by placing the interior lives, memories and experiences of Black women at the centre of her narratives. Kouoh, through her curatorial practice and institutional leadership, similarly challenged established structures of visibility, insisting on the intellectual and artistic significance of voices historically marginalised within dominant cultural institutions. Together, they embody the exhibition’s argument that cultural transformation requires not only recovering neglected histories but also creating new ways of seeing, thinking, and imagining.

In Campos-Pons’s painted world, the two women inhabit a shared symbolic landscape. Their figures become part of a larger ecology of knowledge, connected through roots, branches and blossoms. Neither is confined to conventional portraiture. Instead, their identities expand into something ancestral and mythological, suggesting that their influence extends far beyond the limits of their individual lives.

For Campos-Pons, whose practice has long examined the histories of the African diaspora, displacement, ancestry and the transmission of cultural memory, the installation continues an enduring investigation into how personal histories intersect with collective experience. Her visual language draws on Cuba’s cultural inheritance, the history of the transatlantic slave trade, and the spiritual traditions through which communities have preserved knowledge across generations.

The installation’s development involved intensive experimentation, with drawings, paintings, sculptural models, and sound compositions evolving together. Campos-Pons began with drawings and small models, exploring the magnolia forms through metal and clay before arriving at the finished sculptures. From there, her paintings incorporate watercolour, washes and ink, allowing colour to dissolve into fluid, atmospheric passages in which botanical forms and human figures appear to merge.

Equally important is her collaboration with Malak. As husband and wife, their shared domestic, spiritual and creative lives inform a working relationship in which the boundaries between artistic disciplines are deliberately fluid. In this way, they work as KaMag, developing an approach grounded in sustained dialogue, observation and experimentation. Maria Magdalena Campos-Pons, installation view in Anatomy of the Magnolia Tree for Koyo Kouoh and Toni Morrison (2026), Giardini main pavilion. Photo courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts.

blocks.text: “We have a very beautiful, for us, methodology of work,” Campos-Pons explains in conversation with ART AFRICA. “And we spend hours and hours and hours together doing things.”

As she paints, Malak records the process, observing the development of the drawings, sculptural models and material experiments. Their conversations shape the evolving relationship between image and sound, establishing a creative exchange in which neither discipline takes precedence.
“Everything is together,” Campos-Pons insists. “The sculptures, the paintings, the videos, the sound, and the performance on the stage.”

Malak’s contribution extends this relationship into the physical environment. His 47-minute sound composition incorporates a 40 Hz frequency, intended to create an atmosphere of resonance, contemplation and emotional wellbeing. Since the composition unfolds over a duration considerably longer than most visitors are likely to spend in the gallery, each encounter offers a different passage through the work.

“I wanted to create a sound piece that represented Koyo’s vision in minor keys,” Malak explains. “So the music is designed to be spiritual, to be resonant,” focusing on sound’s capacity to affect emotional and sensory experience.

He associates the 40 Hz frequency with healing and wellbeing, an understanding that informs his compositional approach. Within the installation, the frequency becomes part of a broader artistic exploration of how sound, atmosphere and perception might influence a visitor’s emotional state. The music is not conceived as an accompaniment to the visual work but as an integral component of its sensory architecture. Maria Magdalena Campos-Pons, installation view in Anatomy of the Magnolia Tree for Koyo Kouoh and Toni Morrison (2026), Giardini main pavilion. Photo courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts.

blocks.text: The multisensory ambition extends beyond the auditory. Campos-Pons and Malak introduced fresh guavas, sugarcane, oranges, bananas, mint, vetiver and lavender, creating an environment in which fragrance becomes part of the artwork. In addition, visitors were offered scented packets, allowing the experience to continue through an intimate encounter with the materials.

For Campos-Pons, these elements are not decorative additions. They belong to a conception of artistic experience that refuses to separate the intellectual from the bodily or the spiritual from the material. Although the artists had hoped to incorporate taste, Biennale restrictions prevented this aspect of the work from being realised.

Their approach reflects a deeply held spiritual practice. Campos-Pons describes prayer as part of their daily lives and their creative relationship as one sustained through communication with the natural and cosmic worlds.
“We pray together every single day. And we are spiritual people. We talk to the universe, we talk to the stars, we talk to the water.”

Such statements illuminate an important dimension of Campos-Pons’s wider practice, in which ancestral knowledge, Afro-Caribbean spiritual traditions and the histories of displacement are approached through ritual, material and embodied experience. The artist has consistently explored how memory survives beyond written documentation, finding expression through objects, gestures, images, and inherited cultural practices.

In Venice, this sensibility acquires particular significance through the dedication to Kouoh and Morrison. Both women understood the importance of creating spaces in which experiences excluded from dominant historical narratives could be articulated on their own terms. The installation’s sensory richness proposes an alternative to remembrance as something fixed, solemn or distant. Instead, it argues that memory can be animated through colour, fragrance, sound and the physical presence of the viewer.

The artists extended these concerns beyond the gallery through performances during the Biennale’s opening week, introducing movement, spoken language and collective participation into their tribute to Kouoh. These interventions transformed private grief into a shared public gesture, suggesting that remembrance might become a form of collective renewal.

The installation also reveals a productive tension within In Minor Keys. Kouoh’s exhibition proposes attentiveness to quieter registers of experience, yet Campos-Pons and Malak approach this sensibility through an exuberance of visual and sensory expression. Their magnolias are monumental, their painted imagery expansive, and their performances theatrical. Rather than equating the minor keys with restraint, they interpret them as an invitation to attend to emotional and spiritual frequencies that conventional forms of representation often overlook. Maria Magdalena Campos-Pons, installation view in Anatomy of the Magnolia Tree for Koyo Kouoh and Toni Morrison (2026), Giardini main pavilion. Photo courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts.

blocks.text: Campos-Pons recalls a particularly meaningful response from a fellow artist who emerged from one of their performances feeling unexpectedly calm. This reaction underscored the effect they hoped to achieve.
“Magda, I feel so calm,” the visitor told her.
For Campos-Pons, this response confirmed something fundamental about their intentions. “And I say to Kamal, I say, we did it.”
“In a time of a lot of emotion, a lot of anguish, we wanted to do something mystical, something transcendental that touched you in areas you’re not expecting.”

Her words suggest that the work’s significance cannot be measured solely through its visual or formal qualities. Its ambition lies equally in what visitors carry away, the sensations and memories that might resurface long after the immediate experience has ended.

This understanding resonates with Kouoh’s curatorial vision, which located the transformative possibilities of art in acts of attention, generosity and connection. It also recalls Morrison’s insistence on the enduring power of storytelling to preserve lives, histories and experiences that might otherwise disappear from collective consciousness.

In Anatomy of the Magnolia Tree for Koyo Kouoh and Toni Morrison, Campos-Pons and Malak bring these legacies into a shared imaginative space. Their tribute does not seek to resolve the experience of loss or offer a definitive representation of either woman. Instead, it allows remembrance to remain open, alive and responsive to those who encounter it.

The magnolia, with its associations of beauty, endurance and renewal, becomes an image of this continuity. Its blossoms are at once fragile and monumental, rooted in particular histories yet able to carry meaning across continents and generations. Maria Magdalena and Kamal Malak – KaMag. blocks.text: For KaMag, the work remains an evolving conversation. The artists speak of their curiosity about what might follow, encouraged by audiences who wished the performances had lasted longer. Their collaboration suggests that the experience of Venice is not a conclusion but another stage in an artistic relationship that continues to expand.

What remains most compelling is their conviction that art can create a space in which people experience something beyond the immediately visible or explicable. As Campos-Pons observes, “It’s not to be described, it’s to be experienced, it’s to be there.”

In giving form to the memory of Koyo Kouoh and Toni Morrison, KaMag offers an encounter with the living influence of two women whose work continues to shape the cultural imagination. Their magnolia blossoms are not simply a monument to lives remembered, but an affirmation of the possibilities those lives have made available to others.
